Hot-path review, 2026-11-08

Retained changes:
- Reservation_Timeline::can_fit checks only the requested interval. It no
  longer searches future starts only to reject them.
- The per-pass queue scan uses can_fit(now) after its reservation quota is
  filled. It no longer calculates a future start it cannot use.
The published six-case benchmark uses these changes.

Existing compile-time selection:
- schedule_with_forecast<Timeline> selects exact or grouped forecast code.
- Pending-job status and queue-drain helpers use GroupEvents template
  parameters and if constexpr lambdas; grouping is not checked per job.
- earliest_fit<IncludeEndpoint> selects interval-boundary semantics.
- The main simulation loop already specializes resource accounting, event
  dispatch, periodic backfill, fixed periodic dispatch, and warm-stage behavior.

Remaining runtime choices include backfill policy, queue depth, and planning
resolution. Reservation counts and available capacity change during a scan;
these decisions cannot simply become constants. Backfill policy and fixed
options could be specialized, but each new template dimension adds code.

Measured experiments, not retained:
1. Add RoundRelease to schedule_with_forecast<Timeline, RoundRelease>, choose
   it once at scheduler entry using planning_time_resolution != 0, and use an
   if constexpr lambda for job release calculations. The unrounded path keeps
   (start + estimate) - start to preserve floating-point behavior.
2. Construct baseline m_events with emplace_hint(m_events.end(), time, true)
   instead of emplace(time, true), because baseline event times are ordered.

Both experiments used the same Release flags and Docker environment as the
production benchmark. For each case, one warmup pair preceded 15 measured
pairs, alternating which binary ran first. Schedule and resource hashes match.
constexpr-experiment.json and ordered-insert-experiment.json retain individual
runs and medians. Rounding specialization made grouped replay about 2.8% slower;
other cases changed by roughly 0.3-1.3%. Ordered insertion made grouped replay
about 1.2% slower. These short runs do not prove either change is universally
slower, but provide no consistent benefit for retaining them.

An independent -pg build of the optimized source ran each of grouped OpenPBS,
default OpenPBS, and Fiction hybrid ten times. gprof attributed 85.54% of
sampled grouped CPU and 70.83% of default OpenPBS CPU to the corresponding
schedule_with_forecast instantiation. Helpers are inlined, so this profile
cannot isolate the cost of individual checks inside that function. Profiling
builds and outputs remain in validation/flux/results/timing-20261108; the
instrumented binary was not used for published processing times.
